steps.label: A stone in the corner
steps.caption: A stone at the corner has no intersections outside the board. Only neighbouring empty points inside the board count as liberties.

steps.label: Two liberties
steps.caption: The empty points directly right and below are its two liberties; the diagonal point does not count.

steps.label: White's last liberty
steps.caption: Black surrounds White from three directions. Look for the one empty intersection that still touches White.

steps.label: Capturing White
steps.caption: Black fills that final liberty, leaving White without liberties and removing the white stone.

steps.label: One liberty left
steps.caption: This black stone has only one empty neighbouring point below it. Check the point before extending.

steps.label: Black connects by extending
steps.caption: The new black stone joins the original along a line. The connected group now shares its liberties.

steps.label: Direct connection
steps.caption: The two black stones touch along a horizontal line, so they are already one connected group.

steps.label: Diagonal contact
steps.caption: The nearby lower-right black stone touches only diagonally. It remains a separate group in this task.

steps.label: Shared connecting point
steps.caption: The marked empty intersection is adjacent to both black groups. Playing there would connect them directly.

steps.label: Connected stones
steps.caption: After Black fills the middle point, three stones form a connected group and share liberties.

steps.label: White's possible connection
steps.caption: White could connect the two stones by playing on their shared neighbouring empty point.

steps.label: Black's cutting move
steps.caption: Black takes the common point, blocking that particular direct connection. Another route might still exist.

steps.label: A surrounded empty point
steps.caption: Black would have no liberties in this surrounded point and would capture nothing by playing there.

steps.label: A move Black cannot play
steps.caption: The red cross marks an illegal self-capture in this example, not merely a strategically poor move.

steps.label: Before a ko capture
steps.caption: The central black stone is in atari; White can take its last liberty on the marked point.

steps.label: White captures and creates ko
steps.caption: After White's capture, Black could seem able to recapture immediately, but that would repeat the preceding position.

steps.label: Simple ko prevents immediate recapture
steps.caption: Black cannot immediately retake on the crossed point. Black must play elsewhere first.

steps.label: Returning after moves elsewhere
steps.caption: Black can contest the ko again after an exchange elsewhere. Whether that exchange helps depends on the wider position.

steps.label: Three connected empty points
steps.caption: These three empty intersections currently form one eye space, not two separate eyes.

steps.label: Black occupies the vital point
steps.caption: In this enclosed example, Black splits the eye space, leaving two separate real eyes.

steps.label: Black denies White the vital point
steps.caption: Black takes the central point first, preventing White from immediately making two eyes there; further replies still matter.

steps.label: A point resembling an eye
steps.caption: The central point appears enclosed, but the black stone above has only that point as a liberty.

steps.label: White plays in the false eye
steps.caption: White's move captures the upper black stone, showing why this point is not a secure real eye.

steps.label: Opening stage on 9×9
steps.caption: Look at the corners and available room. These highlights illustrate choices, not a prescribed move order.

steps.label: Middle-game safety first
steps.caption: The central black stone is under pressure. Consider its escape before seeking more territory.

steps.label: Settling the endgame
steps.caption: With larger groups relatively safe, attention can turn to boundaries that still need to be settled.

steps.label: Two development directions
steps.caption: Compare the highlighted directions from the corner with the supporting black stone on the right.

steps.label: Develop toward friendly support
steps.caption: Black develops to the right, where nearby friendly stones may work together.

steps.label: An area of relatively secure territory
steps.caption: The empty points behind the black boundary are more readily countable than unsettled central space.

steps.label: A thick wall facing a weak opponent
steps.caption: The black wall supports nearby fighting, but is not worth a fixed number of territory points.

steps.label: Black's remaining escape route
steps.caption: Before attacking elsewhere, find where Black's pressured group can extend.

steps.label: Black extends outward
steps.caption: The connected black group gains additional room. This does not prove its long-term survival.

steps.label: Locate the straight-three space
steps.caption: First recognise three adjacent empty points inside the surrounding black group.

steps.label: White takes the central vital point
steps.caption: White's move challenges Black's attempt to divide the empty space into two eyes.

steps.label: Black tests a reply
steps.caption: After Black's reply at one end, check the central white stone's final liberty.

steps.label: Verify move legality
steps.caption: White cannot simply fill that final point if it would be self-capture without capturing anything.

steps.label: An unsettled endgame boundary
steps.caption: Compare what happens if Black plays first and what happens if White plays first.

steps.label: Result A: Black first
steps.caption: Black's move shifts the local boundary toward White. Remember this result for comparison.

steps.label: Result B: White first
steps.caption: White's move shifts the boundary the other way. Full scoring depends on the complete position and rules.

steps.label: Two areas to compare
steps.caption: The upper-left fight can continue, but the lower-right black group may need attention more urgently.

steps.label: Black addresses a weakness first
steps.caption: Black extends to give the weak group room, without claiming this is the only whole-board move.

steps.label: A pressured corner group
steps.caption: Compare saving the corner stones with giving them up for gains elsewhere.

steps.label: Option A: a costly rescue
steps.caption: More moves may be required to save the corner group, and the resulting outside position remains uncertain.

steps.label: Option B: outside compensation
steps.caption: The corner stones are abandoned in this illustration while Black seeks outside strength. Judge the whole exchange.

steps.label: A real threat during ko
steps.caption: White has only one liberty left. Black's threatened capture is concrete, although the ko fight is elsewhere.

steps.label: If White ignores the threat
steps.caption: Black can capture the white stone. Whether this threat is worth using depends on the value of the ko.

steps.label: Compare corner directions
steps.caption: Two possible directions are shown. The existing black stone to the right helps explain their different effects.

steps.label: Development with support
steps.caption: Black chooses the direction of nearby support, without claiming that the pattern has a unique correct variation.

steps.label: Identify the turning point
steps.caption: Keep the actual recorded move visible and recall the question you tried to solve at the time.

steps.label: Compare an alternative
steps.caption: The original recorded move is a historical baseline; the other mark is a candidate for comparison, not a proven best move.
